title: How your home network is wired
summary: Find your own addresses, then see the model behind them: private addresses, one subnet, and a router with an inside and an outside.

blocks.title: Your network has an inside, an outside, and one door
blocks.body: Every device in your home has an address on the inside. The router is the door to the outside. Once you can draw that for your own house, every later step in the lab has a place to go.

blocks.heading: Find your address and your router
blocks.code:
# Linux: your address and subnet, then your router (the default gateway)
ip -4 addr show
ip route | grep default

# macOS (Wi-Fi is usually en0)
ipconfig getifaddr en0
route -n get default | grep gateway

# Windows PowerShell or Command Prompt
ipconfig
# look for IPv4 Address, Subnet Mask, and Default Gateway

blocks.heading: Addresses reserved for the inside
columns: What it looks like at home
blocks.caption: These ranges are reserved for private networks and never used on the public internet. If your address starts with one of them, you are looking at the inside.

blocks.heading: One subnet, one router, one outside address
blocks.alt: Four devices with private addresses sit inside one subnet, 192.168.1.0/24. The router has an inside address, 192.168.1.1, and an outside address, 203.0.113.7. The internet sees only the outside address.
blocks.caption: Example addresses. The outside address is from a range reserved for documentation; yours will differ.

blocks.heading: Think of an apartment building
blocks.body: The building has one street address. That is your router's outside address, the only one the internet sees. Inside, every apartment has its own number. Those are the private addresses. A subnet is one floor: everyone on it can knock on each other's doors directly. The front desk is the router. Mail going out gets the building's street address on it, and when replies come back, the desk remembers which apartment asked and delivers it there.

blocks.heading: Three jobs your router does
rows: Forwards anything not on your subnet to the outside
The Default Gateway in the commands above
Hands each device its address when it joins
The router's list of connected devices
Rewrites outgoing traffic to use the one outside address, and maps replies back
The router's status page shows the outside (WAN) address

nodes.title: Laptop sends
nodes.detail: From 192.168.1.23 to a server on the internet.

nodes.title: Not on my subnet
nodes.detail: The laptop hands it to the gateway, 192.168.1.1.

nodes.title: Router rewrites
nodes.detail: Swaps the sender to 203.0.113.7 and remembers the laptop asked.

nodes.title: Server replies
nodes.detail: To 203.0.113.7, the only address it knows.

nodes.title: Router maps back
nodes.detail: Looks up who asked and forwards the reply to 192.168.1.23.

blocks.heading: Which one is a neighbor?
blocks.prompt: Your laptop is 192.168.1.23 on a /24 subnet. Which address is on the same local network?
blocks.explanation: A /24 subnet means the first three numbers must match. 192.168.1.200 shares 192.168.1, so it's a neighbor. The other two are on different networks and would go through the router.
